about: MECH0007 is a 15-credit first-year UCL Mechanical Engineering module taught in Term 2. Following the 2026/27 catalogue, it covers the core of materials science (fundamental properties, bonding, solids, alloys, steel, polymers, crystallography, deformation and dislocation-based strengthening) and links it to the major manufacturing processes that set a material's structure and properties. It is taught in person and assessed by exam (50%), coursework (25%) and a group activity (25%) according to the 2026/27 catalogue.
topics: Basic definitions and fundamental properties for mechanical engineers
Solids: classes of material, structure and defects
Strengthening mechanisms and the role of dislocations

notes.h: Stress, strain and the properties engineers design with
notes.body:
Materials selection starts from a shared vocabulary of properties. This topic defines them precisely and gives typical values so you can sanity-check calculations.

Stress and strain
- Engineering (nominal) stress σ = F/A₀, where A₀ is the original cross-sectional area. Units: Pa (N/m²); MPa (N/mm²) is the everyday unit.
- Engineering strain ε = ΔL/L₀ (dimensionless, often quoted in % ).
- Shear stress τ = F/A for a force parallel to the surface; shear strain γ = tan θ ≈ θ.
- Poisson's ratio ν = −ε_lateral/ε_axial; about 0.3 for most metals (approximate).

Elastic properties
- In the elastic region stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law): σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus. Similarly τ = Gγ (shear modulus G). For isotropic materials E = 2G(1 + ν).
- Approximate Young's moduli: steel about 200–210 GPa, copper about 120–130 GPa, titanium alloys about 110 GPa, aluminium alloys about 70 GPa, glass about 70 GPa, typical polymers about 0.2–4 GPa, diamond over 1000 GPa.
- Worked example: a steel rod, 10 mm diameter and 1 m long, carries 10 kN. A₀ = π × 5² ≈ 78.5 mm², σ ≈ 127 MPa, ε = 127/200 000 ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻⁴, extension ≈ 0.64 mm. With ν = 0.3 the diameter shrinks by about 0.3 × 6.4 × 10⁻⁴ × 10 mm ≈ 1.9 μm.

Strength and ductility
- Yield strength σ_y: stress at the onset of plastic (permanent) deformation; where there is no sharp yield point it is taken as the 0.2 % offset (proof) stress.
- Ultimate tensile strength (UTS): maximum engineering stress, reached when necking begins.
- Ductility: plastic strain to fracture, as % elongation or % reduction in area.

Energy-based properties
- Resilience: elastic energy stored per unit volume up to yield, U_r = σ_y²/(2E). For σ_y = 250 MPa and E = 200 GPa, U_r ≈ 0.16 MJ/m³ (156 kJ/m³).
- Toughness: energy absorbed per unit volume before fracture (area under the whole stress–strain curve). Fracture toughness K_IC measures resistance to crack growth and is the property used in design against brittle fracture.

Hardness
Resistance to localised plastic indentation, measured by Brinell, Vickers or Rockwell tests. Hardness correlates roughly with tensile strength for many metals, which makes it a quick, near non-destructive check.

Physical properties and specific values
- Density ρ: steel about 7.85 g/cm³, titanium about 4.5, aluminium about 2.70 (approximate).
- Specific stiffness E/ρ: steel ≈ 200/7.85 ≈ 25, aluminium ≈ 70/2.70 ≈ 26, titanium ≈ 110/4.5 ≈ 24 GPa per g/cm³. These are almost equal, so changing between these metals does not improve stiffness per unit mass; composites do.
- Others: thermal expansion coefficient, thermal and electrical conductivity, melting point, corrosion resistance, cost.

Exam tips: convert loads to N and areas to mm² to get MPa directly; distinguish stiffness (E) from strength (σ_y) from toughness; quote typical values as approximate.

notes.h: Bonding: why materials behave as they do
notes.body:
The type of bond between atoms explains a great deal about a material: its stiffness, melting point, ductility, conductivity and thermal expansion.

Primary bonds (strong)
- Ionic: electrons transfer from an electropositive atom (e.g. Na) to an electronegative one (e.g. Cl), producing ions held together by electrostatic attraction. Non-directional. Typical of ceramics such as NaCl and MgO: high melting point, hard, brittle, electrically insulating as solids.
- Covalent: neighbouring atoms share electron pairs. Strongly directional, so structures are open and resist distortion. Diamond, silicon, silicon carbide and the carbon backbone of polymer chains. Very hard and high-melting when the covalent network extends in three dimensions.
- Metallic: valence electrons are delocalised into an "electron sea" around positive ion cores. Non-directional, so planes of atoms can slide past one another without breaking the bonding: metals are ductile and good electrical and thermal conductors.
- Many real materials are mixed. Pauling's estimate of ionic character: % ionic ≈ [1 − exp(−0.25(ΔX)²)] × 100, where ΔX is the electronegativity difference. For NaCl (X ≈ 0.93 and 3.16) this is about 71 %; for MgO (1.31 and 3.44) about 68 %.

Secondary bonds (weak)
- Van der Waals forces between fluctuating or permanent dipoles.
- Hydrogen bonds: an especially strong dipole interaction where hydrogen is bonded to O, N or F (water, nylon).
- They hold polymer chains to each other, so they control polymer stiffness and melting/softening temperatures, which is why most polymers are far less stiff than metals.

The bond-energy curve
- The interaction energy U(r) between two atoms combines a long-range attraction and a short-range repulsion. The net force is F = −dU/dr.
- At the equilibrium separation r₀ the force is zero and U is at its minimum; the depth of the well is the bond energy E₀.
- A simple model is the Lennard-Jones potential U = 4ε[(σ/r)¹² − (σ/r)⁶], with minimum at r₀ = 2^(1/6)σ ≈ 1.12σ.

Linking the curve to properties
- Deeper well (higher bond energy) → higher melting point.
- Steeper curvature at r₀ (d²U/dr²) → stiffer bond → higher Young's modulus. Roughly, E scales with the bond stiffness divided by r₀.
- Asymmetry of the well (it is shallower on the stretched side) → mean spacing grows as atoms vibrate more at higher temperature → thermal expansion. Deep, symmetric wells (e.g. strongly covalent ceramics) give low expansion coefficients.

Bonding and property summary
- Ceramics (ionic/covalent): stiff, hard, high melting point, brittle, insulating.
- Metals (metallic): stiff, ductile, tough, conductive.
- Polymers (covalent chains + secondary bonds between chains): low stiffness, low melting or softening point, often ductile or rubbery, insulating.

Exam tips: sketch U(r) and F(r) on the same r-axis and label r₀ and E₀; explain each property link (well depth, curvature, asymmetry) in a sentence; say whether a bond is directional.

notes.h: Solids: material classes, structure and defects
notes.body:
This topic connects bonding to the structures that atoms and molecules form in a solid, and introduces the defects that control so many properties.

Classes of engineering material
- Metals and alloys: metallic bonding, usually crystalline; stiff, strong, ductile, conducting.
- Ceramics and glasses: ionic and covalent compounds (oxides, carbides, nitrides) and silicate glasses; hard, stiff, high-temperature capable, brittle.
- Polymers: long covalently bonded chain molecules held together by secondary bonds (and sometimes cross-links); light, easy to shape, low stiffness and temperature limit.
- Composites: combinations such as carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer or concrete, designed so each phase contributes.

Crystalline, amorphous and semicrystalline
- Crystalline solids have long-range order: a pattern repeats in three dimensions. Most metals and many ceramics.
- Amorphous (non-crystalline) solids have only short-range order: glasses, many polymers, and metallic glasses produced by very fast cooling.
- Semicrystalline polymers contain crystalline regions within an amorphous matrix.
- Single crystals have one continuous lattice (e.g. silicon wafers, turbine blades). Most engineering metals are polycrystalline: many small crystals (grains) with different orientations, separated by grain boundaries.
- Properties of a single crystal can depend on direction (anisotropy); a polycrystal with randomly oriented grains behaves isotropically on average.

Close packing
Metallic and many ionic bonds are non-directional, so atoms pack as densely as their sizes allow. The densest arrangements of equal spheres (FCC and HCP) fill about 74 % of space; covalent solids, constrained by bond directions, form more open structures (diamond cubic about 34 %). Details are in the crystallography topic.

Defects
No real crystal is perfect, and defects are often more important than the perfect structure.
- Point defects: vacancies (missing atoms), self-interstitials, and impurity atoms sitting either on lattice sites (substitutional) or in the gaps between them (interstitial; small atoms such as C, N, H in iron). The equilibrium vacancy fraction rises exponentially with temperature, roughly exp(−Q_v/kT).
- Line defects: dislocations, which allow metals to deform plastically at stresses far below the theoretical strength (see the strengthening topic).
- Planar defects: grain boundaries, twin boundaries, free surfaces and phase boundaries.
- Volume defects: pores, cracks and inclusions, often introduced in processing; they reduce strength and toughness.

Diffusion
Atoms move through solids by jumping into vacancies (substitutional diffusion) or between interstitial sites (interstitial diffusion, much faster). The diffusion coefficient follows an Arrhenius law, D = D₀ exp(−Q/RT), so it rises steeply with temperature. Diffusion drives heat treatments, case hardening (carburising of steel), sintering and the formation of equilibrium phases.

Why this matters
Grain size, impurity content and defect density are set by processing, and in turn control strength, ductility, conductivity and corrosion. This is the "processing → structure → properties" chain at the heart of the module.

Exam tips: give an example of each defect type; distinguish interstitial from substitutional impurities; link each to a property (e.g. grain boundaries strengthen, vacancies enable diffusion).

An alloy is a metal containing one or more other elements. Phase diagrams show which phases are stable at each composition and temperature, and are the map for heat treatment and casting.

Key definitions
- Component: a chemically distinct constituent (e.g. Cu and Ni).
- Phase: a region of uniform structure and composition, separated from others by a distinct boundary (e.g. liquid, an FCC solid solution, a compound).
- Solubility limit: the maximum amount of solute that a phase can dissolve at a given temperature.
- Microstructure: the size, shape and arrangement of phases, seen under a microscope.

Solid solutions
- Substitutional solid solutions form most readily when the Hume-Rothery conditions hold: atomic radii within about 15 %, the same crystal structure, similar electronegativity and similar valence. Cu and Ni satisfy these and are completely soluble in each other.
- Interstitial solid solutions need solute atoms much smaller than the host (C, N, H in iron).

Gibbs phase rule
F = C − P + 2 (degrees of freedom F, components C, phases P). At fixed pressure, as on most metallurgical diagrams, F = C − P + 1. For a binary alloy at a eutectic point three phases coexist, so F = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0: the temperature and all compositions are fixed.

Isomorphous systems (e.g. Cu–Ni)
- Liquidus line: above it, all liquid. Solidus line: below it, all solid (α). Between them, liquid + α coexist.
- Tie line: a horizontal line at the given temperature across the two-phase field. Its ends give the compositions of the two phases.
- Lever rule for phase fractions (by mass, using wt %): with overall composition C₀ and phase compositions C_L and C_α,
  W_α = (C₀ − C_L)/(C_α − C_L), W_L = (C_α − C₀)/(C_α − C_L).
- Example: C₀ = 40 wt% B, C_L = 30 wt% B, C_α = 55 wt% B gives W_α = 10/25 = 0.40 and W_L = 0.60. Note that the fraction of a phase uses the length of the lever arm on the opposite side.

Binary eutectic systems (e.g. Pb–Sn, Al–Si)
- Limited solubility in the solid: two solid phases α and β.
- The eutectic reaction on cooling: L → α + β at a single temperature and composition. The eutectic alloy melts at the lowest temperature in the system, which is why eutectic compositions are used for solders and casting alloys.
- Eutectic microstructure is typically fine alternating lamellae of α and β. Off-eutectic alloys first form primary (proeutectic) α or β, then the remaining liquid transforms to eutectic.

Other invariant reactions
- Eutectoid: one solid → two other solids on cooling (in steel, γ → α + Fe₃C at 727 °C).
- Peritectic: liquid + solid → a different solid.

Equilibrium versus real cooling
Phase diagrams assume equilibrium (slow cooling). Fast cooling limits diffusion, giving cored (compositionally graded) grains or non-equilibrium phases such as martensite in steel.

Exam tips: draw the tie line, read off compositions, then apply the lever rule with the opposite arm; check that the fractions add to 1; state the phase rule result at invariant points.

Steel, iron with up to about 2 wt% carbon (plus other elements), is the most widely used structural metal. Its versatility comes from the iron–carbon phase diagram and from heat treatment.

Iron's allotropes (pure Fe, approximate temperatures)
- α-ferrite: BCC, stable up to 912 °C.
- γ-austenite: FCC, 912–1394 °C.
- δ-ferrite: BCC, 1394 °C to melting at 1538 °C.
FCC austenite dissolves much more carbon (up to about 2.14 wt% at 1147 °C) than BCC ferrite (at most about 0.022 wt% at 727 °C), because its interstitial sites are larger.

The Fe–Fe₃C diagram (key points, approximate)
- Cementite Fe₃C: 6.70 wt% C, hard and brittle.
- Eutectoid point: 0.76 wt% C at 727 °C, γ → α + Fe₃C. (Some texts quote 0.77 or 0.8 wt%.)
- Eutectic point: 4.30 wt% C at 1147 °C, L → γ + Fe₃C (relevant to cast irons).
- Steels are alloys below about 2.14 wt% C; cast irons are above it.

Slow-cooled microstructures
- Eutectoid steel (0.76 wt% C): austenite transforms entirely to pearlite, alternating lamellae of ferrite and cementite.
- Hypoeutectoid steel (less than 0.76 wt% C): proeutectoid ferrite forms first on the austenite grain boundaries, then the remaining austenite (now at 0.76 wt%) becomes pearlite.
- Hypereutectoid steel (0.76–2.14 wt% C): proeutectoid cementite forms first, then pearlite.

Lever-rule example (0.40 wt% C, just below 727 °C)
- Fraction of pearlite W_p = (0.40 − 0.022)/(0.76 − 0.022) ≈ 0.51; proeutectoid ferrite ≈ 0.49.
- Total ferrite (in and outside pearlite) = (6.70 − 0.40)/(6.70 − 0.022) ≈ 0.94; total cementite ≈ 0.06.
More carbon means more pearlite, giving higher strength and hardness but lower ductility.

Non-equilibrium transformations and heat treatment
- Quenching austenite rapidly prevents carbon diffusion. Austenite then shears into martensite, a supersaturated body-centred tetragonal phase. Martensite is very hard and brittle; its hardness rises with carbon content.
- Tempering: reheating martensite to a moderate temperature (below 727 °C) lets carbide particles precipitate, restoring toughness at some cost in hardness. "Quench and temper" is the standard route to high strength with adequate toughness.
- Intermediate cooling rates (or isothermal holds) give fine pearlite or bainite.
- Annealing (slow furnace cooling) gives soft coarse pearlite; normalising (air cooling) gives finer pearlite and a refined grain size.
- Hardenability: the ease of forming martensite through the thickness, increased by alloying elements such as Cr, Mo, Ni and Mn.

Classes of steel
- Plain carbon: low carbon (below about 0.25 wt%, e.g. car body panels, structural sections), medium carbon (about 0.25–0.6 wt%, shafts, gears after heat treatment), high carbon (about 0.6–1.4 wt%, springs, cutting tools).
- Low-alloy steels: small additions for hardenability and strength.
- Stainless steels: at least about 10.5 wt% chromium, which forms a thin protective, self-healing chromium oxide film. Austenitic grades (with Ni, e.g. 18Cr–8Ni) are non-magnetic and ductile; ferritic and martensitic grades are magnetic.
- Tool steels: high carbon plus carbide-forming elements (W, Mo, V, Cr).

Exam tips: label all phase fields and the three key points on the Fe–C sketch; when using the lever rule say which tie line (just above or just below 727 °C) you use; explain martensite as diffusionless, not as a phase on the equilibrium diagram.

Polymers are long-chain molecules built from many repeat units. Their properties depend strongly on chain length, chain architecture and temperature, which makes them very different from metals.

Basic terms
- Monomer: the small molecule from which a polymer is made (e.g. ethylene, C₂H₄).
- Repeat unit (mer): the structural unit repeated along the chain. For polyethylene, –CH₂–CH₂–, molar mass about 28.05 g/mol.
- Degree of polymerisation (DP): the number of repeat units per chain, DP = M_n/m, where m is the repeat-unit molar mass. A polyethylene with M_n = 100 000 g/mol has DP ≈ 100 000/28.05 ≈ 3600.

Making polymers
- Addition (chain-growth) polymerisation: monomers with C=C double bonds add one at a time to a growing chain (polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, polystyrene).
- Condensation (step-growth) polymerisation: functional groups react, often releasing a small molecule such as water (nylons, polyesters).

Molecular weight
- A polymer contains chains of many lengths, so averages are used.
- Number-average: M_n = Σ x_i M_i (x_i = number fraction). Weight-average: M_w = Σ w_i M_i (w_i = weight fraction). M_w ≥ M_n, and the dispersity M_w/M_n measures the spread.
- Example: number fractions 0.25, 0.50, 0.25 at 20 000, 40 000 and 60 000 g/mol give M_n = 40 000; the weight fractions are 0.125, 0.5, 0.375, so M_w = 45 000 and M_w/M_n = 1.125.
- Longer chains mean more entanglement: higher strength and melting point, but harder processing.

Chain architecture
- Linear, branched, cross-linked and network structures. Branching reduces packing (low-density polyethylene is branched; high-density polyethylene is mostly linear, packs better and is stiffer).
- Cross-links are covalent bonds between chains: a few give elastomers (rubbers), many give rigid networks.

Thermoplastics, thermosets and elastomers
- Thermoplastics (PE, PP, PVC, PS, PMMA, nylon): linear or branched chains held by secondary bonds; soften on heating and can be remelted and recycled.
- Thermosets (epoxy, phenolics, polyester resins): heavily cross-linked networks formed during curing; do not melt and degrade on strong heating; stiffer and more heat resistant.
- Elastomers (natural rubber, silicone): lightly cross-linked, used above their glass transition; large recoverable strains.

Crystallinity and thermal transitions
- Polymers may be amorphous or semicrystalline (chains fold into ordered lamellae in parts). Crystallinity raises density, stiffness and chemical resistance, and is favoured by regular, linear chains.
- Glass transition temperature T_g: below it the amorphous regions are glassy and stiff; above it chain segments move and the material becomes rubbery or leathery. Examples (approximate): polystyrene about 100 °C, PMMA about 105 °C, natural rubber about −70 °C.
- Melting temperature T_m applies only to crystalline regions, and T_m > T_g.

Mechanical behaviour
- Young's moduli are low (very roughly 0.2–4 GPa for bulk thermoplastics, approximate) because deformation largely stretches secondary bonds between chains.
- Viscoelasticity: response depends on time and rate; polymers creep under constant load at room temperature and relax under constant strain.
- Properties change sharply near T_g, so service temperature is critical.

Exam tips: always state the repeat-unit mass when computing DP; distinguish T_g (amorphous) from T_m (crystalline); explain thermoplastic vs thermoset in terms of cross-linking and recyclability.

Crystallography describes the regular arrangement of atoms in crystals. It tells you how densely atoms pack, which planes slip, and how X-ray diffraction identifies a structure.

Lattices and unit cells
- A crystal lattice is a regular 3-D array of points; the unit cell is the smallest repeating block that reproduces the crystal by translation. Its shape is set by the lattice parameters a, b, c and angles α, β, γ.
- There are seven crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices; first-year work concentrates on cubic and hexagonal structures.

The common metallic structures (hard-sphere model, atomic radius R)
- Simple cubic (SC): 1 atom per cell, a = 2R, coordination number 6, atomic packing factor (APF) = π/6 ≈ 0.52. Rare in metals (polonium).
- Body-centred cubic (BCC): 2 atoms per cell, atoms touch along the body diagonal so a = 4R/√3, coordination number 8, APF ≈ 0.68. Examples: α-Fe, Cr, W, Mo.
- Face-centred cubic (FCC): 4 atoms per cell, atoms touch along a face diagonal so a = 2√2 R, coordination number 12, APF ≈ 0.74. Examples: Cu, Al, Ni, γ-Fe, Au.
- Hexagonal close-packed (HCP): 6 atoms per hexagonal cell (2 per primitive cell), coordination number 12, APF ≈ 0.74, ideal c/a ≈ 1.633. Examples: Mg, Ti (at room temperature), Zn.
- FCC and HCP are both close packed; they differ only in stacking of close-packed layers: ABCABC… (FCC) versus ABAB… (HCP).

Theoretical density
- ρ = nA/(V_c N_A), where n = atoms per cell, A = atomic mass (g/mol), V_c = a³ for cubic cells and N_A ≈ 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
- Copper (FCC, R ≈ 0.128 nm, A ≈ 63.55 g/mol): a = 2√2 × 0.128 ≈ 0.362 nm, ρ ≈ 4 × 63.55/((0.362 × 10⁻⁷ cm)³ × 6.022 × 10²³) ≈ 8.9 g/cm³ (measured about 8.96).
- α-Iron (BCC, R ≈ 0.124 nm, A ≈ 55.85): a ≈ 0.286 nm and ρ ≈ 7.9 g/cm³.

Miller indices
- Directions [uvw]: subtract tail from head coordinates (in units of a, b, c), clear fractions to the smallest integers, enclose in square brackets; negatives with a bar (written here as −1). A family of equivalent directions is ⟨uvw⟩.
- Planes (hkl): find the intercepts on the axes in units of a, b, c, take reciprocals, clear fractions, enclose in round brackets. A plane parallel to an axis has an infinite intercept, so index 0. Families are written {hkl}. If the plane passes through the origin, shift the origin first.
- In cubic crystals the direction [hkl] is perpendicular to the plane (hkl).
- Interplanar spacing (cubic): d_hkl = a/√(h² + k² + l²).
- Close-packed planes and directions: {111} and ⟨110⟩ in FCC; in BCC the densest are {110} planes and ⟨111⟩ directions.

X-ray diffraction
- Bragg's law: nλ = 2d sin θ, where θ is the angle between the incident beam and the planes.
- Example: BCC iron (a ≈ 0.2864 nm), (110) planes, d = 0.2864/√2 ≈ 0.2025 nm. With Cu Kα radiation (λ ≈ 0.1542 nm) the first-order peak is at sin θ = 0.1542/(2 × 0.2025) ≈ 0.381, θ ≈ 22.4°, so 2θ ≈ 44.8°.
- Not every (hkl) reflects: in BCC, peaks appear only when h + k + l is even; in FCC, only when h, k, l are all odd or all even.

Exam tips: show the geometry that links a to R; count atoms per cell carefully (corners count ⅛, faces ½, body 1); report θ or 2θ explicitly in diffraction answers.

This topic follows a metal through a tensile test and explains, at the atomic scale, what happens in the elastic and plastic regimes.

The tensile test
- A standard specimen is pulled at a steady rate; load and extension are recorded and converted to engineering stress and strain.
- Elastic region: linear, slope E, fully recoverable. Atoms are displaced slightly from their equilibrium spacing and spring back.
- Yield: plastic (permanent) deformation begins. Some steels show a distinct upper and lower yield point; otherwise the 0.2 % proof stress is used.
- Work (strain) hardening: beyond yield, more stress is needed to keep deforming as dislocations multiply and tangle.
- Ultimate tensile strength: the maximum engineering stress. Beyond it, deformation localises in a neck, the load falls, and the specimen eventually fractures.
- On unloading from the plastic region the specimen springs back elastically along a line parallel to the original elastic slope; the remaining strain is permanent.

True stress and strain
- True stress σ_T = F/A (instantaneous area); true strain ε_T = ln(L/L₀).
- Before necking (constant volume): σ_T = σ(1 + ε) and ε_T = ln(1 + ε). Example: engineering stress 300 MPa at 20 % strain gives σ_T = 360 MPa and ε_T ≈ 0.182.
- The true stress keeps rising to fracture; the drop on the engineering curve is a geometric effect of the shrinking neck.

Why plastic deformation happens at low stress
- Shearing a perfect crystal would require breaking all bonds across a plane at once. The theoretical shear strength is roughly G/2π (crude estimate), thousands of MPa for steel, yet real metals yield at a few hundred MPa or less.
- The explanation is dislocations: line defects that let a plane slip one row of atoms at a time, so only a few bonds are broken at any instant.

Slip
- Slip occurs on specific crystallographic planes and directions, the slip system, usually the most densely packed plane and direction.
- FCC: {111}⟨110⟩, 12 slip systems; plenty of easy systems, so FCC metals (Cu, Al, Ni, Au) stay ductile even at low temperature.
- BCC: ⟨111⟩ slip directions on {110} (and other) planes; many systems but they need thermal activation, so BCC metals such as steel can become brittle at low temperature (ductile–brittle transition).
- HCP: at room temperature mainly basal slip (0001)⟨11−20⟩, only 3 systems, so many HCP metals (Mg, Zn) have limited ductility.

Schmid's law
- A tensile stress σ along an axis resolves onto a slip system as τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ, where φ is the angle between the load and the slip-plane normal and λ the angle between the load and the slip direction.
- Slip begins when τ_R reaches the critical resolved shear stress τ_CRSS, so the single-crystal yield stress is σ_y = τ_CRSS/(cos φ cos λ)max.
- The Schmid factor cos φ cos λ is at most 0.5 (φ = λ = 45°). Example: σ = 50 MPa at φ = λ = 45° gives τ_R = 25 MPa. If φ = 60° and λ = 30°, the factor is 0.433, so an illustrative CRSS of 20 MPa is reached at about 46 MPa. (Real CRSS values vary widely with purity: very roughly 0.5–1 MPa for pure copper or aluminium single crystals, approximate.)

Other deformation and failure modes
- Twinning: a region of crystal shears into a mirror-image orientation; important in HCP and at low temperature or high strain rate.
- Ductile fracture: necking, void formation and growth, cup-and-cone surfaces. Brittle fracture: rapid crack propagation with little plastic deformation, often by cleavage along crystal planes.

Exam tips: sketch and label the stress–strain curve (E, σ_y, UTS, fracture, elastic recovery); quote Schmid's law with both angles defined; explain the theoretical vs actual strength gap with dislocations.

notes.h: Strengthening mechanisms and the role of dislocations
notes.body:
Plastic deformation in metals happens by dislocation motion. Every common strengthening method works the same way: it makes dislocations harder to move. The price is usually some loss of ductility.

Dislocations
- Edge dislocation: an extra half-plane of atoms ending inside the crystal. The Burgers vector b (the closure failure of a circuit around the dislocation) is perpendicular to the dislocation line.
- Screw dislocation: the lattice is sheared into a helical ramp around the line; b is parallel to the line.
- Mixed dislocations have both characters along their length.
- Dislocations glide on their slip plane under a resolved shear stress; when a dislocation crosses the whole crystal it leaves a step of one Burgers vector. Edge dislocations can also climb out of their plane by diffusion at high temperature.
- Dislocations carry strain fields (compression above an edge's slip plane, tension below) which interact with other dislocations and with solute atoms.
- Dislocation density, total line length per volume, is very roughly 10¹⁰–10¹² m⁻² in annealed metals and up to about 10¹⁵–10¹⁶ m⁻² in heavily cold-worked metals (approximate).

1. Grain-size reduction
- Grain boundaries block slip because the slip planes change orientation across them. Finer grains mean more barriers.
- Hall–Petch relation: σ_y = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2), where d is the grain diameter.
- Example (illustrative values): σ₀ = 70 MPa, k_y = 0.74 MPa m^½: for d = 25 μm, σ_y = 70 + 0.74/√(25 × 10⁻⁶) = 70 + 148 = 218 MPa; for d = 100 μm, σ_y = 144 MPa.
- Unusually, grain refinement improves toughness as well as strength.

2. Solid-solution strengthening
- Solute atoms of a different size distort the lattice; their strain fields interact with those of dislocations, pinning them. Examples: Zn in Cu (brass), Mg in Al, C and N in Fe.

3. Strain (work) hardening
- Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which tangle and obstruct each other, so the flow stress rises.
- Cold work is quantified as %CW = (A₀ − A_d)/A₀ × 100. Drawing a 10 mm diameter wire to 8 mm gives %CW = (100 − 64)/100 × 100 = 36 %.
- Ductility falls as %CW rises.

4. Precipitation (age) hardening
- Solution treat to dissolve the alloying element, quench to trap it in a supersaturated solid solution, then age at a moderate temperature so fine precipitates form (e.g. Al–Cu, Al–Mg–Si alloys, some nickel superalloys).
- Fine, closely spaced precipitates impede dislocations strongly. Ageing too long (overageing) coarsens them, increases spacing and lowers strength.
- Dispersion strengthening uses insoluble particles such as oxides, stable at high temperature.

5. Martensitic transformation (steels)
- The supersaturated BCT structure of martensite and its high defect density give very high hardness; tempering trades some of this for toughness.

Recovery, recrystallisation and grain growth
Heating a cold-worked metal:
- Recovery: some dislocations annihilate or rearrange; internal stresses relax.
- Recrystallisation: new strain-free grains nucleate and grow, removing work hardening. It occurs above a recrystallisation temperature, very roughly 0.3–0.5 of the absolute melting temperature (approximate), lower for heavily cold-worked or very pure metals.
- Grain growth: on further heating the grains coarsen, lowering strength.

Exam tips: for each mechanism, name the obstacle and explain how it impedes dislocations; quote Hall–Petch with units; recall that only grain refinement raises both strength and toughness.

Manufacturing turns materials into parts, and in doing so sets their microstructure and therefore their properties. Choosing a process depends on the material, the shape, the tolerance and finish needed, the production volume and cost.

Casting
- Molten metal is poured or injected into a mould and solidifies to shape.
- Sand casting: cheap tooling, large parts, rough finish, low to medium volumes.
- Die casting: molten metal (usually Al, Zn or Mg alloys) injected under pressure into steel dies; excellent finish and high rates, but costly tooling.
- Investment (lost-wax) casting: ceramic shell around a wax pattern; complex, accurate parts such as turbine blades.
- Structure: columnar and equiaxed grains, possible porosity and segregation. Faster cooling gives finer grains and better properties.

Forming (deformation processing)
- Forging (compressive shaping between dies), rolling (thickness reduction between rolls), extrusion (pushing through a die to make constant cross-sections), drawing (pulling through a die for wire and tube) and sheet-metal forming (bending, deep drawing, stamping).
- Hot working is done above the recrystallisation temperature (itself very roughly 0.3–0.5 of the absolute melting point, approximate): low forces, large deformations, no work hardening, but poorer surface finish and dimensional control because of oxidation and thermal contraction.
- Cold working is below it: better finish and tolerances and the part is strengthened by work hardening, but forces are higher and ductility falls; intermediate annealing may be needed.
- Forging aligns the grain flow with the part's shape, which improves fatigue and impact performance compared with machining from bar.

Machining (material removal)
- Turning, milling, drilling, grinding. Precise tolerances and good finishes on almost any metal, but wasteful of material and slow for large volumes. Often used to finish cast or forged parts.

Joining
- Fusion welding (arc, MIG/TIG, laser) melts the parent metal locally; the heat-affected zone (HAZ) next to the weld can be weakened, hardened or embrittled depending on the alloy.
- Brazing and soldering use a filler metal with a lower melting point that wets the joint without melting the parts.
- Mechanical fastening (bolts, rivets) and adhesive bonding avoid heating the parts.

Powder processing
- Powder metallurgy: press metal powder to shape, then sinter below the melting point so particles bond by diffusion. Near-net shape, minimal waste, controlled porosity (self-lubricating bearings); also the main route for ceramics and hard metals such as tungsten carbide.

Additive manufacturing
- Parts are built layer by layer from a digital model: powder-bed fusion for metals (laser or electron beam), material extrusion (fused filament) for polymers, and others. It allows complex internal geometries and lightweight lattices, but build rates are slow and parts may contain porosity, residual stress and anisotropy that need post-processing.

Polymer processing
- Injection moulding (melt injected into a cooled mould; high volume, complex shapes), extrusion (continuous profiles, pipe, film), blow moulding (hollow bottles), thermoforming (heated sheet formed over a mould). Thermosets are shaped by compression or transfer moulding, or as resins in composite layup, before curing.

Heat treatment as a process step
Annealing, normalising, quenching and tempering, and age hardening are often part of the process route; surface treatments such as carburising harden the surface of steel parts.

Process selection summary
- One-off or low volume: machining, sand casting, additive manufacturing.
- High volume: die casting, forging, stamping, injection moulding.
- Material constraints: brittle materials cannot be formed plastically, so ceramics are powder processed and cast irons are cast.

Exam tips: for any process, be ready to state the materials it suits, its typical volume, and how it affects microstructure and properties; contrast hot and cold working clearly.

questions.q: Which property is given by the area under the elastic part of the stress–strain curve only, up to yield?
questions.why: Resilience is the elastic energy stored per unit volume up to yield, σ_y²/(2E). Toughness is the area under the whole curve up to fracture, including plastic work. Young's modulus is the slope of the elastic region, not an area. Hardness is resistance to indentation, measured by a separate test.

Lateral strain = −νε ≈ −5.9 × 10⁻⁴, so each 20 mm side shrinks by about 0.012 mm. Since 125 MPa is below the 280 MPa yield strength, the bar deforms elastically and recovers fully on unloading.

questions.q: Which feature of the interatomic potential energy curve U(r) mainly determines Young's modulus?
options: The curvature of the well at the equilibrium spacing
The value of U at very large separation
The depth of the energy well
questions.why: Stiffness is the rate at which the restoring force grows with small displacements from r₀, i.e. d²U/dr² at r₀, so the curvature sets E. Well depth is the bond energy, which correlates with melting point. Asymmetry explains thermal expansion. U at large separation is zero by convention for all bonds and carries no information about stiffness.

questions.q: Why are metals generally ductile while ionic ceramics are brittle?
options: Metallic bonds are weaker than ionic bonds
Metals have a lower density than ceramics
Ionic ceramics contain no dislocations at all
Metallic bonding is non-directional, so planes can slip without breaking the bonding pattern; in ionic crystals slip would bring like charges together
questions.why: In a metal the electron sea bonds every ion to its neighbours whatever their exact arrangement, so planes can slide; in an ionic crystal sliding by part of a lattice spacing brings like-charged ions face to face, so slip is very difficult and cracks propagate instead. Saying metallic bonds are weaker is not the reason (many metals have very high bond energies). Density has no direct bearing on ductility (many metals, such as steel, are denser than common ceramics). Ceramics do contain dislocations; they simply move with great difficulty.

questions.q: Sketch and label the interatomic potential energy U(r) and force F(r) for a pair of atoms. Use the sketch to explain how melting point, Young's modulus and thermal expansion relate to the curve.
markScheme: U(r): repulsion rising steeply at small r, attraction at larger r, minimum at r₀ with depth E₀
F = −dU/dr; F = 0 at r₀
Deeper well (larger E₀) → higher melting point
Greater curvature at r₀ (slope of F at r₀) → higher E
Asymmetric well → mean spacing increases with vibration amplitude → thermal expansion
questions.modelAnswer: U(r) falls from large positive values at small r (repulsion), passes through a minimum of depth E₀ at r₀, and rises towards zero at large r (attraction dominating but weakening). F = −dU/dr is zero at r₀, negative (attractive) beyond it, and strongly repulsive at small r. The well depth E₀ is the energy needed to separate the atoms, so deeper wells mean higher melting points. The curvature of U at r₀, equal to the slope of F there, is the bond stiffness, so a steeper curvature gives a higher Young's modulus. Because the well is steeper on the compressed side than on the stretched side, larger thermal vibrations shift the mean spacing outwards, which is thermal expansion; deep, symmetric wells expand least.

questions.q: Carbon atoms dissolved in iron are an example of which type of defect?
questions.why: Carbon atoms are much smaller than iron atoms and sit in the gaps between them, so they are interstitial impurities. A vacancy is a missing host atom, not an added foreign one. Substitutional impurities replace host atoms on lattice sites and need a similar atomic size, which carbon lacks. A grain boundary is a planar defect between crystals, not an individual atom.

questions.q: Why does interstitial diffusion usually proceed much faster than substitutional diffusion in the same metal?
options: Interstitial atoms are small and there are many empty interstitial sites, so a neighbouring site is almost always free
Substitutional atoms cannot move at all
Interstitial diffusion requires a vacancy next to the atom
questions.why: Small interstitial atoms can jump to an adjacent interstitial site, and such empty sites are plentiful, so jumps happen often. They are not heavier; they are usually lighter. Needing a vacancy is the condition for substitutional diffusion, which is exactly why it is slower (vacancies are scarce). Substitutional atoms do move, via vacancies, just less often.

questions.q: Describe the four main categories of crystal defect, giving an example of each and one property that each affects.
markScheme: Point: vacancy/interstitial/impurity — affects diffusion, solid-solution strength, conductivity
Line: dislocation — enables plastic deformation, ductility, work hardening
Planar: grain boundary/twin — impedes dislocations (strength), corrosion paths
Volume: pores/cracks/inclusions — reduce strength and toughness
questions.modelAnswer: Point defects are zero-dimensional: vacancies, self-interstitials and impurity atoms; vacancies enable diffusion and solute atoms raise strength (solid-solution strengthening) and lower electrical conductivity. Line defects are dislocations, whose motion is how metals deform plastically, so they govern ductility and work hardening. Planar defects include grain boundaries and twin boundaries; grain boundaries block dislocations, so finer grains give higher yield strength, and they can be preferential corrosion paths. Volume defects such as pores, cracks and inclusions act as stress concentrators that reduce strength and toughness.

questions.q: At a given temperature an alloy of overall composition 40 wt% B lies in a liquid + α field, with C_L = 30 wt% B and C_α = 55 wt% B. What is the mass fraction of α?
questions.why: W_α = (C₀ − C_L)/(C_α − C_L) = (40 − 30)/(55 − 30) = 0.40. 0.60 is the liquid fraction, from using the near arm (55 − 40)/25 for α. 0.25 is (55 − 30)/100, the tie-line length as a fraction of 100 %. 0.73 is 40/55, the overall composition divided by the α composition, which is not the lever rule.

questions.q: In a binary alloy at constant pressure, how many degrees of freedom are there at the eutectic point?
questions.why: With the fixed-pressure phase rule F = C − P + 1 = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0: three phases (L, α, β) coexist only at one temperature and fixed compositions. 1 comes from counting only two phases (2 − 2 + 1), as in a two-phase field. 2 uses the general rule F = C − P + 2 with P = 2. 3 uses F = C − P + 2 with P = 1, i.e. a single-phase region with pressure free.

questions.q: Explain, with a sketch of a binary eutectic phase diagram, the microstructures formed on slow cooling of (a) the eutectic composition and (b) a hypoeutectic composition.
markScheme: Diagram: two solid-solution fields α and β, liquidus meeting at eutectic point, eutectic isotherm
(a) Eutectic alloy stays liquid down to T_E then transforms L → α + β at constant temperature
(a) Microstructure: fine lamellar α + β eutectic
(b) Hypoeutectic: primary α forms between liquidus and T_E, liquid enriches towards eutectic composition
(b) At T_E remaining liquid → eutectic; final structure primary α grains in eutectic matrix (fractions by lever rule just above T_E)
questions.modelAnswer: The diagram has α (rich in A) and β (rich in B) solid-solution fields at the sides, liquidus lines falling to the eutectic point, and a horizontal eutectic isotherm at T_E. (a) An alloy of eutectic composition remains fully liquid until T_E, then transforms isothermally by L → α + β; diffusion over short distances produces a fine lamellar mixture of α and β. (b) A hypoeutectic alloy (between the α solubility limit and the eutectic composition) begins to solidify at the liquidus, forming primary α. As it cools the α grows and the remaining liquid becomes richer in B, reaching the eutectic composition at T_E. That liquid then transforms to eutectic, giving primary α grains surrounded by lamellar eutectic; the lever rule just above T_E gives the fraction of primary α.

questions.q: A plain carbon steel with 0.40 wt% C is slowly cooled to just below 727 °C. What is the approximate mass fraction of pearlite? (Use 0.022 wt% and 0.76 wt% C for the ferrite and eutectoid compositions.)
questions.why: W_p = (0.40 − 0.022)/(0.76 − 0.022) ≈ 0.378/0.738 ≈ 0.51. 0.94 is the total ferrite fraction (from the tie line to 6.70 wt% C), which includes ferrite inside the pearlite. 0.53 is 0.40/0.76, ignoring the small carbon solubility of ferrite. 0.49 is the proeutectoid ferrite fraction, using the opposite arm.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of tempering a quenched steel?
options: To increase toughness by letting carbides precipitate from brittle martensite
To dissolve all the carbon into austenite
questions.why: Tempering reheats martensite below the eutectoid temperature so carbon leaves the supersaturated lattice as fine carbides, restoring toughness. Dissolving carbon into austenite is austenitising, carried out above 727 °C before quenching. Martensite is formed by the quench itself, not by tempering. Corrosion resistance comes from chromium content, not heat treatment.

questions.q: Describe the microstructures produced when a 0.40 wt% C steel is (a) slowly cooled from 900 °C and (b) water-quenched from 900 °C, and compare their mechanical properties.
markScheme: At 900 °C the steel is fully austenitic (above the A3 line for 0.4 wt% C)
(a) Slow cooling: proeutectoid ferrite forms on austenite grain boundaries below the A3 line, then remaining austenite → pearlite at 727 °C; about 49 % ferrite, 51 % pearlite
(a) Moderate strength, good ductility and toughness
(b) Quenching suppresses diffusion: austenite → martensite (BCT, supersaturated in C)
(b) Very hard and strong but brittle; usually tempered afterwards
questions.modelAnswer: At 900 °C a 0.40 wt% C steel is single-phase austenite. (a) On slow cooling, proeutectoid ferrite nucleates on the austenite grain boundaries once the A3 line is crossed (roughly 800 °C for this composition, approximate), and the remaining austenite becomes richer in carbon until, at 727 °C, it has the eutectoid composition and transforms to pearlite. The lever rule gives about 49 % proeutectoid ferrite and 51 % pearlite. This gives moderate strength with good ductility and toughness. (b) Water quenching is too fast for carbon diffusion, so austenite transforms by shear to martensite, a body-centred tetragonal phase supersaturated with carbon. It is much harder and stronger but brittle, so it is normally tempered to recover toughness.

questions.q: A polyethylene sample has M_n = 100 000 g/mol. The repeat unit –CH₂–CH₂– has molar mass 28.05 g/mol. What is the degree of polymerisation?
questions.why: DP = M_n/m = 100 000/28.05 ≈ 3570. About 7130 uses the CH₂ unit (14.03 g/mol) instead of the full C₂H₄ repeat unit. About 2.8 × 10⁶ multiplies instead of dividing. About 1790 uses a repeat-unit mass of 56 g/mol, doubling the true value.

questions.q: Which statement about thermosets is correct?
options: They have a crystalline melting point but no glass transition
They are cross-linked networks that do not melt on reheating
They soften and can be remoulded on heating
They are held together only by van der Waals forces between chains
questions.why: Thermosets are covalently cross-linked during curing, so the chains cannot slide past each other when heated; they decompose instead of melting. Softening and remoulding describes thermoplastics. Being held only by secondary forces is also the thermoplastic picture. Thermosets are usually amorphous, so they show a glass transition rather than a crystalline melting point.

questions.q: Distinguish between thermoplastics, thermosets and elastomers in terms of molecular structure, behaviour on heating and typical uses, and explain what happens to an amorphous thermoplastic as it is heated through T_g.
markScheme: Thermoplastic: linear/branched chains, secondary bonds; softens/melts, recyclable; e.g. PE bottles, PP
Thermoset: dense covalent cross-link network; does not melt, chars; e.g. epoxy adhesives, composite matrices
Elastomer: light cross-linking, used above T_g; large recoverable strain; e.g. tyres, seals
Below T_g: glassy, stiff, brittle; above T_g: chain segments mobile, modulus drops by orders of magnitude, rubbery/leathery
Further heating of amorphous thermoplastic → viscous flow (no sharp melting point)
questions.modelAnswer: Thermoplastics consist of linear or branched chains held together by secondary bonds and entanglement; on heating the chains slide, so they soften and can be remelted and recycled (PE packaging, PP mouldings). Thermosets are dense covalent networks formed when a resin cures; heating cannot separate the chains, so they char rather than melt; they are used as adhesives and composite matrices (epoxy). Elastomers are lightly cross-linked and used above their T_g; the chains uncoil under load and the cross-links pull them back, giving large reversible strains (tyres, seals). An amorphous thermoplastic below T_g is glassy, stiff and relatively brittle. On heating through T_g, segmental chain motion begins and the modulus falls by orders of magnitude to a rubbery or leathery state; further heating leads to viscous flow without a sharp melting point.

questions.q: What is the atomic packing factor of a body-centred cubic metal (hard-sphere model)?

questions.q: A single crystal is loaded in tension at 50 MPa. The slip-plane normal is at 60° and the slip direction at 30° to the load axis. What is the resolved shear stress on the slip system?
questions.why: τ_R = σ cos φ cos λ = 50 × cos 60° × cos 30° = 50 × 0.5 × 0.866 ≈ 21.7 MPa. 25 MPa assumes the maximum Schmid factor of 0.5 (both angles 45°). 43.3 MPa uses cos 30° only, forgetting the plane-normal factor. 12.5 MPa uses cos 60° twice, as if both angles were 60°.

questions.q: Why do FCC metals such as aluminium and copper usually remain ductile at low temperatures while many BCC steels become brittle?
options: BCC metals have no slip systems
FCC metals have lower Young's moduli than all BCC metals
FCC metals have more easy close-packed slip systems ({111}⟨110⟩) that operate without much thermal activation
questions.why: FCC crystals have 12 close-packed slip systems with a low, temperature-insensitive resistance to dislocation glide. BCC slip needs thermal activation, so at low temperature the yield stress rises until cleavage fracture wins. FCC metals certainly contain dislocations; that is how they deform. BCC metals do have slip systems, just harder ones at low temperature. Modulus is not the controlling factor (FCC nickel, about 200 GPa, is stiffer than BCC niobium or vanadium, roughly 100–130 GPa, approximate).

questions.q: Sketch an engineering stress–strain curve for a ductile metal, labelling E, the 0.2 % proof stress, UTS and fracture. Explain the difference between the engineering and true stress–strain curves after the UTS.
markScheme: Linear elastic region with slope E
0.2 % offset construction for proof stress
Work hardening to UTS (maximum engineering stress), then necking and fracture
Engineering stress uses original area so it falls after necking
True stress uses instantaneous area and keeps rising to fracture
questions.modelAnswer: The curve rises linearly with slope E, curves over at yield, where the 0.2 % proof stress is found by drawing a line parallel to the elastic slope from 0.2 % strain, then rises more slowly as the metal work hardens up to the maximum, the UTS. Beyond the UTS a neck forms, the load falls and the specimen fractures. Engineering stress divides the load by the original area, so after necking it falls even though the material in the neck is still hardening. True stress divides by the instantaneous (much smaller) neck area, so the true curve continues to rise until fracture.

questions.q: A steel obeys Hall–Petch with σ₀ = 70 MPa and k_y = 0.74 MPa m^½ (illustrative values). What is its yield strength for a grain size of 25 μm?
questions.why: σ_y = 70 + 0.74/√(25 × 10⁻⁶) = 70 + 0.74/0.005 = 218 MPa. 70.1 MPa drops the micro prefix, taking d = 25 m (0.74/√25 ≈ 0.15). 74.7 MPa puts d in millimetres (0.74/√0.025 ≈ 4.7) although k_y is in MPa m^½. 148 MPa is the grain-boundary term alone, forgetting to add σ₀.

questions.q: A copper wire is drawn from 10 mm to 8 mm diameter. What is the percentage cold work?
questions.why: %CW = (A₀ − A_d)/A₀ × 100 = (10² − 8²)/10² × 100 = 36 % (the π/4 cancels). 20 % uses the diameters instead of the areas. 64 % is the remaining area fraction A_d/A₀. 56 % comes from (A₀ − A_d)/A_d = 36/64, dividing by the final area instead of the original.

questions.q: Explain why all strengthening mechanisms in metals involve impeding dislocation motion, and describe how precipitation hardening works, including why overageing reduces strength.
markScheme: Plastic deformation = dislocation glide; yield stress set by stress needed to move dislocations
Obstacles (grain boundaries, solute, other dislocations, precipitates) raise that stress
Solution treatment dissolves solute; quench traps it in supersaturated solid solution
Ageing forms fine, closely spaced precipitates that pin or must be cut/bypassed by dislocations
Overageing: precipitates coarsen, spacing increases, dislocations bow between them more easily → strength falls
questions.modelAnswer: Metals yield when dislocations start to glide, so the yield stress is the stress needed to move dislocations through the crystal; anything that obstructs them raises it. Precipitation hardening uses a heat treatment in three steps. Solution treatment at high temperature dissolves the alloying element; quenching traps it in a supersaturated solid solution; ageing at a moderate temperature lets very fine, closely spaced precipitates form. Dislocations must either cut through these particles or bow around them, both of which need extra stress, so strength rises sharply. If ageing continues too long or too hot, the precipitates coarsen and their spacing grows, so dislocations can bow between them at lower stress and strength falls; this is overageing.

questions.q: Which process is best suited to producing 100 000 complex thermoplastic housings per year?
questions.why: Injection moulding gives complex thermoplastic parts with good finish at very high rates once the mould is made. Sand casting is a metal process for lower volumes. Machining from solid would be slow and wasteful at this volume. Fused-filament printing builds each part layer by layer and is far too slow and costly per part for this volume.

questions.q: Compared with hot rolling, cold rolling a steel strip typically gives:
options: Higher strength, better surface finish and tighter tolerances, but reduced ductility
Lower strength and poorer surface finish
No change in properties, only a thinner strip
questions.why: Cold rolling is below the recrystallisation temperature, so the strip work hardens (higher strength, lower ductility) and, without oxide scale or thermal contraction, gives a better finish and tolerance. Lower strength and poorer finish describes hot rolling relative to cold. Saying properties are unchanged ignores work hardening. Larger grains and higher ductility describes annealing or hot working, not cold rolling.

questions.q: A connecting rod for a car engine could be made by sand casting, by forging or by machining from bar. Compare the three routes in terms of microstructure, mechanical performance, material use and suitability for high-volume production.
markScheme: Sand casting: cheap tooling, near-net shape, but coarse grains/porosity reduce fatigue strength; rough finish
Forging: grain flow follows the part, refined structure, best fatigue and impact performance; dies costly but suited to high volume
Machining from bar: accurate but wasteful, slow, grain flow cut across; suits prototypes/low volume
Conclusion: forging (followed by finish machining) preferred for a highly stressed, high-volume part
Mentions need for some finish machining or heat treatment
questions.modelAnswer: Sand casting gives a near-net shape with cheap tooling, but the as-cast structure is relatively coarse and may contain porosity and segregation, lowering fatigue strength, and the finish is rough. Forging deforms hot metal between dies; it refines the grain structure, closes porosity and makes the grain flow follow the rod's shape, giving the best fatigue and impact resistance. Dies are expensive but the cycle is fast, so it suits high volumes. Machining from bar gives accurate dimensions but wastes much material, is slow for volume production and cuts across the grain flow. For a highly stressed, high-volume part such as a connecting rod, forging followed by finish machining of critical surfaces (and any heat treatment) is the usual choice.

questions.q:
(a) Sketch the steel-relevant part of the Fe–Fe₃C phase diagram (up to about 2 wt% C), labelling phase fields, the eutectoid point and the key temperatures and compositions. [6]
(b) For a 0.40 wt% C plain carbon steel slowly cooled from 900 °C, describe the microstructural development and calculate the mass fractions of proeutectoid ferrite, pearlite, total ferrite and total cementite just below 727 °C (use 0.022, 0.76 and 6.70 wt% C). [8]
(c) Explain how quenching and tempering could be used to produce a shaft from this steel with high strength and adequate toughness. [6]
markScheme: (a) Fields: γ (FCC), α (BCC), α + γ, γ + Fe₃C, α + Fe₃C; A1 line at 727 °C
(a) Eutectoid at ~0.76 wt% C, 727 °C; max C in α ~0.022 wt%; γ solubility ~2.14 wt% at 1147 °C; α→γ at 912 °C for pure Fe
(b) Fully austenitic at 900 °C; proeutectoid α forms on γ grain boundaries below A3; remaining γ enriched to 0.76 wt% then → pearlite at 727 °C
(c) Austenitise above A3, quench rapidly → martensite (diffusionless, BCT, hard but brittle)
(c) Temper below 727 °C: carbides precipitate, internal stresses relax, toughness rises, hardness falls somewhat; temperature chosen to balance
(c) Mentions hardenability/section size, risk of quench cracking or distortion
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The sketch shows austenite γ (FCC) at high temperature, bounded below by the A3 line falling from 912 °C at 0 wt% C to the eutectoid point (≈ 0.76 wt% C, 727 °C), and by the A_cm line rising from the eutectoid to about 2.14 wt% C at 1147 °C. Below 727 °C (the A1 line) lie α + Fe₃C. Between the A3 line and A1 is α + γ; to the right of A_cm is γ + Fe₃C. The α field is a thin sliver near the left axis, with maximum solubility ≈ 0.022 wt% C at 727 °C.

(b) At 900 °C the 0.40 wt% C steel is single-phase austenite. On cooling, it crosses the A3 line (roughly 800 °C, approximate) and proeutectoid ferrite nucleates on the austenite grain boundaries. As ferrite, which holds little carbon, grows, the remaining austenite becomes richer in carbon, its composition following the A3 line down to 0.76 wt% at 727 °C. At 727 °C that austenite transforms to pearlite. Just below 727 °C, using the tie line from 0.022 to 0.76 wt% C: W_α' (proeutectoid) = (0.76 − 0.40)/(0.76 − 0.022) = 0.36/0.738 ≈ 0.49 and W_pearlite = (0.40 − 0.022)/0.738 ≈ 0.51. Using the tie line from 0.022 to 6.70 wt% C: total ferrite = (6.70 − 0.40)/(6.70 − 0.022) = 6.30/6.678 ≈ 0.94, total cementite ≈ 0.06. The final structure is light-etching ferrite grains with dark pearlite colonies, in roughly equal proportions.

(c) Heat the shaft above the A3 temperature to form uniform austenite, then quench in water or oil. Diffusion is suppressed, so austenite transforms by shear into martensite, a body-centred tetragonal structure supersaturated with carbon: very hard and strong but brittle and highly stressed. Then temper by reheating to a chosen temperature below 727 °C: carbon precipitates as fine carbides, internal stresses relax and toughness and ductility rise, with some loss of hardness. Higher tempering temperatures give tougher, softer results, so the temperature is chosen to balance strength and toughness for the shaft's duty. A plain 0.4 wt% C steel has limited hardenability, so thick sections may not harden through; low-alloy steels with Cr or Mo are used where full-section hardening is needed. Quench distortion and cracking are risks to control.

questions.q:
(a) Copper is FCC with atomic radius 0.128 nm and molar mass 63.55 g/mol. Calculate its lattice parameter, theoretical density and atomic packing factor. [6]
(b) State the slip system of FCC metals and explain why it is chosen. A copper single crystal is loaded in tension along an axis making 60° with the slip-plane normal and 30° with the slip direction; τ_CRSS = 0.5 MPa (approximate). Find the tensile stress at which slip starts. [6]
(c) Polycrystalline copper is much stronger than this single-crystal value. Explain two reasons, and use the Hall–Petch relation σ_y = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2) with σ₀ = 25 MPa and k_y = 0.11 MPa m^½ (illustrative values) to estimate the yield strength for d = 10 μm and d = 100 μm. [8]
markScheme: (b) {111}⟨110⟩: most densely packed planes and directions; smallest Burgers vector and widest plane spacing, so lowest resistance to slip
(b) Schmid factor = cos 60° cos 30° ≈ 0.433; σ = 0.5/0.433 ≈ 1.15 MPa
(c) Grain boundaries block slip; differently oriented grains require multiple slip systems for compatibility; dislocation interactions / work hardening
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) In FCC atoms touch along the face diagonal: √2 a = 4R, so a = 2√2 × 0.128 ≈ 0.362 nm. a³ = (0.362 × 10⁻⁷ cm)³ ≈ 4.75 × 10⁻²³ cm³. With 4 atoms per cell, ρ = 4 × 63.55/(4.75 × 10⁻²³ × 6.022 × 10²³) ≈ 254.2/28.6 ≈ 8.9 g/cm³ (measured 8.96). APF = 4 × (4/3)πR³/(2√2 R)³ = π/(3√2) ≈ 0.74.

(b) FCC metals slip on {111} planes in ⟨110⟩ directions. These are the most densely packed planes (so they are the most widely spaced and the easiest to shear) and the most densely packed directions (shortest Burgers vector, so the lowest lattice resistance and dislocation energy). There are 12 such systems. The Schmid factor is cos 60° × cos 30° = 0.5 × 0.866 = 0.433, so slip begins when σ = τ_CRSS/0.433 = 0.5/0.433 ≈ 1.15 MPa.

(c) In a polycrystal, grain boundaries interrupt slip planes, so dislocations pile up against them and extra stress is needed to start slip in neighbouring grains. Also, each grain must deform compatibly with its differently oriented neighbours, which requires several slip systems to operate at once (some with low Schmid factors), and the resulting dislocation interactions cause rapid work hardening; impurities and solute add further strengthening. Hall–Petch: for d = 10 μm, d^(−1/2) = 1/√(10⁻⁵) ≈ 316 m^(−1/2), so σ_y ≈ 25 + 0.11 × 316 ≈ 25 + 34.8 ≈ 60 MPa. For d = 100 μm, d^(−1/2) = 100 m^(−1/2), so σ_y ≈ 25 + 11 = 36 MPa. Both are far above the ~1 MPa single-crystal value, and finer grains give higher strength.
